name: base-from-member
intent: Name the C++ Ron's Member/base-from-member technique: C++ constructs direct bases before ordinary members, so a base whose constructor needs object-owned state can receive it only if that state is itself a base — move the member into a private holder base, list the holder before the dependent base in the base-specifier list, and the holder (and with it the member) is fully constructed when the dependent base's initialiser reads its value or address.
problem: An ordinary derived member cannot be constructed before a direct base. If that base's constructor reads from, invokes through, or otherwise requires the member's value or identity, passing its address or reference from the member-initialiser list reaches storage whose object's lifetime has not begun; merely storing a pointer is only safe if the base makes no lifetime-dependent access until later. The dependency is circular: the base needs the member, and the member follows the bases.
context: Use this only in C++ hierarchies you control when a real base must consume object-owned state during construction. C++ initializes virtual bases first, then direct bases in base-specifier order, then members in declaration order; a private holder can exploit only the direct-base portion. This is a local layout and ABI decision, not a general data-sharing abstraction.
benefits: Makes a dependent base constructible from object-owned data without changing that base: the base keeps its ordinary constructor signature and receives the holder's value or address after the holder exists.
Adds no separate holder allocation: the carrier is an inline subobject, although its member may own resources or allocate internally.
The mechanism is small and reusable: Boost.Utility supplies boost::base_from_member, while a hand-written holder works when construction or special-member behavior needs custom logic.
One holder can serve any number of dependent bases declared after it, and a discriminator (Boost's UniqueID tag or a distinct holder type) allows several subobjects of the same member type.
It makes an otherwise invisible constraint explicit: the base-specifier order becomes construction order, so a reviewer can see why the holder exists and which bases depend on it.
Reverse destruction keeps the carrier alive until dependent direct bases are destroyed; every dependent destructor still needs an explicit check of that lifetime contract.
tradeoffs: The constraint lives in the base-specifier list, not in the member-initialiser list: reordering the bases, or inserting a new base in front of the holder, silently restores the invalid dependency and may produce undefined behaviour.

The class stops being an aggregate and gains a base it does not want in its type; the member and the helper's names become findable through the derived class (name lookup precedes access checks), and any non-private inheritance exposes the idiom in the interface.

Repeated members of the same type are ill-formed without a discriminator: base classes are unnamed, so a class cannot have two direct bases of the same member type — the library template needs its UniqueID tag, the hand-written form needs distinct holder types.

Layout and ABI change when a member moves into a base, and the helper adds a constructor to forward — plus, for a non-copyable member, either lost copy/move operations or hand-written special members.

It is a hierarchy-level commitment for what is often a value: a constructor parameter, a C++11 delegating constructor, or composition is simpler when the dependent base does not need the member's identity or lifetime.
Tooling sees the trick: serializers, bindings, debuggers and class-layout tools now show an extra, unnamed base, and templates in the derived class must be written around it.

Taking the address of a carrier's member through a qualified base name (for example, &pbase0_type::member) yields a pointer-to-member rather than a raw pointer; use this-> qualification or an accessor for the latter.

participants.responsibility: The newly introduced base class whose only job is to own the based-member and construct it from the forwarded arguments; declared before the dependent base so it is initialised first, and kept private because it is an implementation detail.

The data member the other base needs — a value, or storage whose address or reference is bound into that base. After the move it lives in the holder base and is named from the derived class as the base's member (directly, through a using-declaration, or through an accessor).

The base that must be initialised from the member (an ostream requiring the streambuf, an allocator bound to the object's storage). Its initialiser reads the member's value or address and is only correct because the holder base was constructed first.

Controls the order by the order in which it lists its bases: forwards constructor arguments to the holder base first, then constructs the dependent base with the member, and keeps the idiom out of its own public interface.

Optional but required for repetition: boost::base_from_member's int UniqueID template argument — or a distinct hand-written holder struct per member — when one class needs several subobjects of the same member type.

use_cases: Stream wrappers: an iostream base (std::ostream) constructed from a stream-buffer carrier, the canonical fdostream/fdoutbuf example documented by Boost and Josuttis.
Boost.Spirit's multi_pass iterator uses boost::base_from_member to construct shared iterator state before its policy base, so the policy base can consume the state pointer safely.
Boost.MultiIndex's multi_index_container uses boost::base_from_member for a rebound allocator carrier that must precede index and header bases in the hierarchy.
Allocator- or arena-aware types: a dependent base holds an allocator or arena handle bound to storage inside the same object, so the object owns the storage without an extra holder allocation.
Bases that need the address of object-owned storage: a view, lock, atomic or monitor base wraps or instruments a member and therefore needs its identity rather than a copy.
Adapters whose base API stores an interior pointer or reference during construction, when a composition member would not provide the required base relationship or access to protected hooks.

Ported legacy hierarchies: the class previously allocated the member on the heap purely to satisfy the base, and the idiom removes that extra allocation while keeping the base's constructor unchanged.
CRTP finalizer patterns: a CRTP base must flush or finalize a resource during its destructor, so the resource belongs in a carrier that precedes the CRTP base and therefore outlives it.
Multi-carrier dependency chains: when CarrierB requires a resource from CarrierA, declare CarrierA first and CarrierB next; the base list is the dependency order.

Standard-library-like stream wrappers are a useful audit target, not a mandate: current libc++ basic_stringstream keeps its string buffer as a member and passes its address to basic_iostream because the stream base only stores the pointer during construction.
Identity-bound policy objects: a policy base must be given the exact state object the most-derived constructor owns, rather than a value copy or a separately allocated replacement.

C++17 std::optional is a late-initialization alternative when the dependent object is not required to be a real base; base-from-member remains the choice when substitution, protected hooks or is_base_of checks are part of the contract.

Boost.Iostreams' stream: detail::stream_base derives from boost::base_from_member<stream_buffer<Device, Tr, Alloc>> ahead of the stream base, so every device adapter (file_stream, filter_stream) binds its ostream to a buffer that already exists — verified in stream.hpp.

Debug/tee streams built on the hand-written form of the idiom, e.g. the flipcode dbgstream: a private left-most carrier holds the streambuf feeding an OutputDebugString sink while the std::ostream base initialises after it.
avoid_when: The dependency is only a value that can be computed before construction: pass a constructor parameter or static helper result, and use a C++11 delegating constructor to centralize overloads.
Composition would do: if the dependent type is not conceptually a base of this object, hold it as a member constructed after the data, or wrap it behind a delegating interface.
The hierarchy crosses an ABI boundary (a published base list or library interface), so moving a member into a base forces users to recompile or the order cannot be guaranteed.

The constructor set is large or the class is heavily templated: every constructor and special member must forward through the helper base, and the unnamed base multiplies deduction and overload-resolution corner cases.

The language already gives you an explicit construction phase or constructor call (for example, Swift's phase 1 or a Python/Ruby initializer body), so the C++ ordering trick imports a problem the language does not have.

The carrier is stateless and zero-sized, and the dependent base does not need it during construction: C++20 [[no_unique_address]] can preserve member-style composition; it does not replace this idiom for a live value or address dependency.
The dependent base is virtual: virtual bases are initialized first by the most-derived class, so a direct holder cannot push a carrier ahead of it; restructure the hierarchy instead.
anti_patterns: Reaching for the idiom when a constructor parameter would do: relocating a real member into a base to silence an initialisation-order complaint when the value could be computed before the call or passed in.

Letting the helper become part of the public hierarchy: inheriting from boost::base_from_member publicly, or documenting the helper base as an extension point, so an implementation detail turns into an interface.

Reordering or extending the base-specifier list afterwards (style cleanup, adding an interface or a mixin) without checking where the helper sits — the dependent base is then constructed first and the object is invalid.
Hand-rolling one holder base per member type where the library template, or plain composition, would do, duplicating forwarding constructors and copy/move semantics.
Smuggling state into a base for behaviour it should not have — a base that pulls the member's address to escape encapsulation, or to self-register the object unasked.

Letting a dependent base retain an interior pointer through a default move: the destination may still point into the source carrier, so use observes the wrong object or becomes dangling when the source dies.
Using NULL instead of nullptr in pre-C++11 code: the null-pointer literal has type int, causing overload-resolution ambiguity when a holder or dependent base accepts both integral and pointer types.

Keeping the holder after C++11 delegating constructors or a simple constructor parameter already solves a value-only dependency: the extra base adds layout, copy/move and review burden without fixing an identity or lifetime requirement.
design_principles: Work with the language's initialisation model instead of against it: base subobjects are the part of the object guaranteed to be constructed before members, so a member that must precede a base has to become a base.
Information hiding: the helper base and the based-member are implementation details — private inheritance, nothing exposed through the class's interface.
Single responsibility: the holder base owns exactly one member and constructs it; it carries no behaviour of its own.
Prefer composition over inheritance where the relationship is incidental — reach for this idiom only when the base genuinely needs object-owned data.

Make implicit constraints explicit: the compiler cannot generally check the dependency's construction order, so document the holder's position and test that the dependent base receives the intended identity.
C++20 [[no_unique_address]] is appropriate for a stateless carrier when no base constructor depends on it; it is not an ordering substitute for a live non-empty member.
Zero-overhead principle: the idiom exists to solve a specific ordering problem; do not add behavior to the carrier base beyond owning and constructing the member.
best_practices: Declare the holder base first and privately, and comment that its position is load-bearing: the base list is initialisation order, the member-initialiser list is not.

Prefer the library form (boost::base_from_member<MemberType, UniqueID>) over hand-written holders; write the holder yourself only when the member's construction needs more than argument forwarding, or when the dependency is unacceptable.
Use the tag parameter (or a distinct holder type) whenever one class needs two members of the same type, and give the member a documented name or accessor instead of reaching into the base blindly.
Keep the idiom invisible: private inheritance, no public member, and no documentation of the helper as an extension point.
Add a runtime test or invariant check that the dependent base sees the holder's intended value or address; a static_assert can document type relationships but cannot prove base construction order.
Re-check every change to the base list and to the constructor set: new bases, virtual inheritance and added constructors all pass through the helper and can invalidate the ordering.

For zero-size policy types in C++20 or later, evaluate [[no_unique_address]] on the regular member first; only use inheritance when the carrier needs a non-empty type or when the base must be a real base (for example, for std::is_base_of checks).

In multi-carrier hierarchies, document the dependency chain explicitly: the order is the contract, and a later reader inserting a new carrier in the wrong place will introduce invalid construction with no useful diagnostic.

Watch the pointer-to-member-pointer trap: when taking the address of the carrier's member for use as a raw pointer, qualify with this-> or use a helper accessor to ensure the correct type is obtained.

Consider destruction explicitly: verify that each dependent base releases or flushes through the carrier while the carrier's member is still alive; do not assume every base destructor uses the resource safely.

Use typedefs or type aliases for the carrier and dependent bases to make member qualification readable: typedef boost::base_from_member<X> pbase_type; otherwise every use of member requires the long qualified form.

Use static_assert only for what it can prove (for example, that a required holder type remains a base); pair it with a runtime construction test for the ordering invariant rather than pretending an assertion can observe initialization order.

For pre-C++11 code, use an explicit cast (static_cast<T*>(nullptr)) instead of NULL when a constructor overload could match both pointer and integral arguments; in C++11 and later, nullptr eliminates this ambiguity.

After a move operation on the derived class, any raw pointer stored in the dependent base that points into the carrier's member may still address the source object — document this invariant and define or delete move operations accordingly.
In teams, add the base-ordering constraint to the class's code-review checklist: any change to the base-specifier list must verify that the holder remains first among bases that depend on it.

For template uses of the idiom, ensure constructor template arguments are already the correct type before they reach the forwarded call — C++ cannot explicitly specify template arguments for a templated constructor, so explicit conversions may be necessary at the call site.

Boost.Spirit multi_pass — production use of boost::base_from_member to construct shared iterator state before its policy base: https://github.com/boostorg/spirit/blob/develop/include/boost/spirit/home/support/iterators/multi_pass.hpp

Boost.MultiIndex multi_index_container — production use of a base-from-member allocator carrier before index and header bases: https://github.com/boostorg/multi_index/blob/131e3427ae53a6353411088b4a04bdff81d8e806/include/boost/multi_index_container.hpp

libc++ basic_stringstream source — a useful counterexample showing that an implementation can keep the string buffer as a member when the stream base only stores its pointer: https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/blob/main/libcxx/include/sstream

WG21 N1986, Delegating Constructors — proposal motivating the C++11 feature and its limits (a delegating initializer cannot also initialize other bases or members): https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2006/n1986.pdf

Artima, C++ Coding Standards, Item 34 — prefer composition to inheritance, with nonpublic inheritance justified when construction/destruction order requires it: https://www.artima.com/articles/c-coding-standards
Wikibooks, More C++ Idioms/Base-from-Member — intent, circular-initialization motivation, and hand-written holder example: https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Base-from-Member
cppreference, Constructors and member initializer lists — practical construction-order and delegating-constructor reference: https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/language/constructor

Boost.Iostreams stream.hpp source — detail::stream_base : protected base_from_member<stream_buffer<Device, Tr, Alloc>>, a production use of the idiom behind every boost::iostreams::stream device adapter: https://github.com/boostorg/iostreams/blob/develop/include/boost/iostreams/stream.hpp

flipcode, 'Debug Stream' — hand-written base-from-member in production: a private left-most carrier holds the streambuf that feeds an OutputDebugString sink before the std::ostream base initialises: https://www.flipcode.com/archives/Debug_Stream.shtml
isocpp.org C++ FAQ, Constructors — construction order (direct bases left to right, then members) and the initialization-order fiasco that motivates the idiom: https://isocpp.org/wiki/faq/ctors

Boost review discussion, 'Re: [boost] Review: Base from Member' (2001) — contemporary critique that the helper communicates intent only marginally better than a hand-written holder and can obfuscate the class: https://lists.boost.org/Archives/boost/2001-08-15542.php

related_patterns_notes.empty-base-optimization: removes storage cost for an empty base; base-from-member instead orders a non-empty carrier before a dependent base.
related_patterns_notes.barton-nackman: uses CRTP for operators and friendship; base-from-member uses a holder base solely to control construction order.
related_patterns_notes.non-copyable-mixin: supplies a non-copyability policy through inheritance; base-from-member stores construction-dependent state and may inherit non-copyability incidentally.
related_patterns_notes.pimpl: hides representation behind an indirection; base-from-member keeps the carrier inline and changes the hierarchy instead.
related_patterns_notes.crtp: gives a base static access to its derived type; base-from-member can be paired with CRTP when a carrier must outlive that base.
related_patterns_notes.intrusive-reference-counting: embeds ownership operations and state in the object; base-from-member only arranges lifetime before a dependent base.
related_patterns_notes.no-unique-address: compresses a stateless member without inheritance; it cannot replace base-from-member when a base constructor needs that member.
related_patterns_notes.mixin: composes reusable behavior through inheritance; base-from-member's holder should have no behavior and remain private.
related_patterns_notes.factory-persona: separates construction policy into a factory or helper; base-from-member solves an in-object base/member ordering dependency instead.
related_patterns_notes.tag-dispatching: selects compile-time overloads by tag; the UniqueID tag in base-from-member only differentiates repeated holder base types.
related_patterns_notes.virtual-dispatch: selects runtime overrides; base-from-member concerns construction order and does not make constructor-time virtual calls safe.
